first_principles_question: Who controls the digital action before value can happen?
what_it_tells_us: Technology demand is about identity, security, workflow routing, data movement, AI infrastructure, and permissioned action, not only apps.
example_company_types: cybersecurity, cloud, communications, payments, software platforms, AI infrastructure
proof_boundary: Does not prove all software demand is durable or AI-driven.
writing_use: Use as the technology expansion theme.

first_principles_question: What does a person pay someone else to do because time, energy, skill, or emotional bandwidth is scarce?
what_it_tells_us: Services reveal how households and businesses spend for convenience, status, relief, mobility, attention, and outsourced effort.
example_company_types: restaurants, lodging, travel, casinos, advertising, transportation, entertainment, staffing
proof_boundary: Does not prove consumer health; service growth may reflect stress, substitution, debt, or price.
writing_use: Add as the largest missing cultural theme.

first_principles_question: Who gets paid because other companies cannot afford for work to stop?
what_it_tells_us: Industrial companies sell continuity: equipment availability, parts, technical support, distribution, and project execution.
example_company_types: equipment rental, MRO, electrical distribution, HVAC, construction, fleet support
proof_boundary: Backlog, revenue, or utilization does not by itself prove cash conversion or project return.
writing_use: Keep as a main article pillar.

first_principles_question: What does a household keep buying because it protects a feeling or routine the household does not want to lose?
what_it_tells_us: Consumer goods reveal spending that protects normalcy, cleanliness, safety, small control, entertainment, trust, and identity.
example_company_types: food, packaging, beauty, personal care, toys, household goods, apparel
proof_boundary: Sales do not automatically prove brand strength, pricing power, or durable margins.
writing_use: Add as a household psychology theme.

first_principles_question: Which physical inputs become hard to get when many parts of the economy try to build at once?
what_it_tells_us: Power, housing, infrastructure, food, electronics, defense, and industrial buildout depend on plain physical inputs.
example_company_types: steel, copper, lumber, fertilizer, chemicals, aggregates, packaging inputs
proof_boundary: End-market demand does not guarantee pricing power for every materials company.

first_principles_question: Who organizes care when human need, payment rules, labor limits, and medical capacity collide?
what_it_tells_us: Healthcare demand is obvious; value is in arranging care that can be staffed, reimbursed, authorized, scheduled, and trusted.
example_company_types: payers, PBMs, dialysis, home care, hospice, labs, devices, drugstores
proof_boundary: Volume growth does not prove better care, better outcomes, or better cash quality.
writing_use: Keep and expand with cash and quality boundaries.

first_principles_question: Who controls the route between energy supply and energy use?
what_it_tells_us: Energy value depends on moving molecules through gathering, processing, pipelines, storage, refining, LNG, exports, contracts, and tariffs.
example_company_types: midstream, LNG, refining, upstream, NGLs, terminals, storage
proof_boundary: Volume growth does not prove high-quality cash or durable project return.
writing_use: Use as the energy expansion theme.

first_principles_question: Whose promise is being transformed into someone else's funding?
what_it_tells_us: Financial companies route savings, premiums, deposits, fees, receivables, and borrowed funds into assets, borrowers, policies, and collateral pools.
example_company_types: asset managers, insurers, banks, BDCs, card lenders, payment networks
proof_boundary: AUM, premiums, deposits, and commitments are not named-cash proof.

first_principles_question: Who controls a location that someone else must use?
what_it_tells_us: Real estate value can come from scarce sites, power access, towers, logistics locations, lodging demand, medical geography, and shelter need.
example_company_types: REITs, towers, lodging, logistics property, data-center sites, medical offices
proof_boundary: Owning property does not prove pricing power or cash durability.

first_principles_question: Who gave permission to spend, and who is obligated to pay through bills?
what_it_tells_us: Utilities turn public need into capital plans, regulatory approval, assets, recovery, customer bills, reliability, and affordability debates.
example_company_types: electric utilities, gas utilities, water utilities, grid operators
proof_boundary: Approved capex does not automatically become collected cash or fair customer value.
writing_use: Keep as a main power/grid pillar.

first_principles_question: Who can turn scarce labor into repeatable service?
what_it_tells_us: Many sectors depend on recruiting, training, scheduling, dispatching, retaining, and supervising scarce skilled labor.
example_company_types: healthcare, restaurants, lodging, construction, field service, delivery, utilities
proof_boundary: Automation does not remove every labor constraint.

first_principles_question: Who gets paid because someone else needs a reliable gatekeeper?
what_it_tells_us: Trust is paid for through security, authorization, custody, brand reliability, food safety, payment reliability, insurance promises, and infrastructure dependability.
example_company_types: cybersecurity, payments, healthcare, consumer brands, insurance, utilities, custody
proof_boundary: Trust is not only a soft brand claim; it needs repeat behavior, lower risk, or payment proof.
writing_use: Add as a cross-sector unifying theme.
